justice: Sidewalk space exists on both sides, suggesting some baseline allocation for pedestrians alongside vehicle lanes (equity of space).

Frequent curbside occupation by parked cars and multiple parked/standing scooters reduces usable pedestrian clear width, effectively disadvantaging people walking with strollers or carrying goods (equity/accessibility).
No clearly marked barrier-free features (e.g., visible curb ramps or tactile paving) can be confirmed at the edges shown, limiting universal access for all users (accessibility).
Traffic appears to operate as shared space without obvious protected zones for walking/cycling, which can create de facto priority for drivers over non-motorized users (fairness).
safety: No visible crosswalks, stop lines, or pedestrian-priority markings in the segment shown, increasing uncertainty and conflict risk at driveways/intersections ahead (traffic safety).
On-street parking and curbside parked scooters narrow the effective roadway and sightlines, creating dooring risk and reducing visibility between drivers and people walking/cycling (conflict risk).
Absence of a protected bike lane or physical separation means cyclists likely mix with motor vehicles in a narrow corridor (cycling crash risk).
Active storefront edges provide some informal surveillance ('eyes on the street'), which can modestly support perceived safety in daytime (personal security).
livability: Ground-floor shops and continuous building frontage indicate mixed-use activity that can support daily needs and street vitality (everyday convenience).
Presence of pedestrians and small-scale activity near shopfronts suggests the street functions as a local commercial/social corridor (vitality).
Clutter at the edges (scooters, items near storefronts) reduces the quality of the public realm and can limit comfortable social use of sidewalks (public-space usability).
Lack of visible seating/rest areas and limited greenery reduces opportunities for lingering and casual social interaction (stayability).
sustainability: Car dominance is evident (multiple cars parked and traveling), indicating a mobility pattern that is less supportive of low-carbon mode share (transport sustainability).
No clear public-transport infrastructure (e.g., bus stop signage/shelter) is visible, limiting sustainable modal options in this segment (mode support).
Very limited vegetation and no visible green infrastructure (trees, planters, bioswales) reduce ecological and heat-mitigation benefits (urban greening).
While scooters/bikes are present, there is no dedicated cycling facility or organized parking, which weakens sustained low-carbon travel support (active mobility support).
aesthetics: Consistent two-story street wall and repeating facade rhythm create a coherent streetscape and human-scale enclosure (visual coherence).
Traditional/vernacular architectural elements (balconies, railing patterns, lantern-like fixtures) add character and identity (place character).
Visible weathering/stains on some facades and edge clutter from parked scooters and stored items reduce perceived upkeep (maintenance).
Street is relatively clean and uncluttered in the centerline, supporting a legible, orderly visual axis (streetscape legibility).
comfort: Minimal tree canopy and little shade provision means low thermal comfort during hot or sunny periods (thermal comfort).
Sidewalk paving appears uneven/patchwork in places and is frequently obstructed by scooters and parked vehicles, reducing physical walking comfort (physical comfort).
Narrow effective pedestrian zone next to moving/parked cars can feel stressful, lowering psychological comfort for people walking (psychological comfort).
Active shopfronts and building enclosure can provide some sense of place and orientation, supporting comfort despite traffic presence (psychological comfort).
walkability: Continuous sidewalks exist on both sides, providing a basic walking network along the corridor (continuity).
Frequent curbside obstructions (scooters, stored items, parked cars encroaching near the edge) reduce effective width and force detours (path quality).
Lack of visible marked crossings and pedestrian-priority cues reduces safe connectivity across and along the street (crossing safety/connectivity).
Active frontage with shops increases walking attractiveness and destination access, partially offsetting infrastructure weaknesses (destination support).
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bicycle lane markings are visible; cyclists likely share a narrow lane with cars (level of traffic stress).
On-street parking creates door-zone hazards and unpredictable merging, discouraging cycling (safety/comfort).
Scooters appear parked along the sidewalk rather than in organized bike/scooter parking, indicating weak end-of-trip facilities for bikes (parking/support facilities).
Roadway looks relatively straight with moderate speeds implied by narrowness, which helps somewhat, but without separation cycling remains uncomfortable for most users (network comfort).
